summaries.gardner: Coca-Cola is a classic 'Rule Maker' rather than a Rule Breaker: it is the top dog in a mature industry, not a first mover in an emerging one, and its revenue grew only 2% in 2025. It does have strong price momentum (up about 37% in the past year) and one of the world's best-known brands, but it lacks the innovation and growth Gardner seeks.
summaries.buffett: Coca-Cola is one of Buffett's signature holdings: Berkshire Hathaway owns 400 million shares, and the company has a simple business, an enduring brand moat, a 61.6% gross margin and 64 straight years of dividend increases. The weak point today is price: at about 27 times earnings and a 3.6% free-cash-flow yield there is little margin of safety.
summaries.munger: Munger long praised Coca-Cola as a business with an unbeatable brand and distribution system, and thinking backwards there are few ways for it to fail. He would likely judge it a wonderful business at a full price, with health trends and slow volume growth as the main risks to watch.
summaries.lynch: Coca-Cola is Lynch's textbook stalwart: a big, steady company with a simple story (sell more drinks at higher prices, mostly abroad). Its PEG ratio of about 3.6 is well above Lynch's comfort level, and the stock is anything but overlooked.
summaries.fisher: Coca-Cola scores well on Fisher's points about sales and marketing skill, profit margins and long-term outlook, and it keeps adding new brands such as fairlife and BodyArmor. It is weaker on his growth points, since volume was flat in 2025 and research and development plays only a small role.
summaries.graham: Coca-Cola passes Graham's tests for size, a dividend record going back over a century, profits every year and EPS growth (diluted EPS rose from $1.67 in 2015 to $3.04 in 2025). It fails the valuation tests badly: about 34 times three-year average earnings and P/E times P/B of about 290, versus Graham's limits of 15 and 22.5.
summaries.thiel: Coca-Cola built a near-monopoly position in branded cola and a distribution network rivals cannot match, which fits Thiel's points on durability and distribution. It has no proprietary technology ten times better than rivals and no hidden secret, so it scores poorly on his technology and timing questions.
summaries.gerstner: Coca-Cola is not the kind of high-growth, technology-driven company Gerstner usually backs, with organic revenue growth of about 5% guided for 2026. Its steady earnings and raised 2026 guidance help, but at about 26.5 times forward earnings the valuation is rich for its growth.
summaries.druckenmiller: Coca-Cola has strong price momentum (up about 37% in a year versus about 17% for SPY) and raised its 2026 guidance after a strong Q2, which Druckenmiller would note. But it lacks the earnings acceleration and big macro tailwind he typically seeks, and comparable EPS growth of 9-10% is not explosive.
summaries.smith: Coca-Cola fits Terry Smith's 'good company' test well: a high gross margin of 61.6%, ROIC of about 20%, resilient consumer demand and steady cash generation, and Fundsmith has long owned consumer staples like it. At about 28 times free cash flow, the 'don't overpay' rule is the question.
summaries.greenblatt: Coca-Cola has a high return on capital (ROIC about 20%), but its earnings yield is only about 3.8% at an EV/EBIT of about 26.5. It would rank only mid-pack on a Magic Formula screen.
summaries.akre: Coca-Cola is strong on Akre's first leg (an extraordinary business with high returns) and decent on management, but weak on reinvestment: it pays out about two-thirds of its earnings as dividends because it cannot reinvest much at high returns.
summaries.pabrai: Coca-Cola offers a very low risk of permanent loss, but there is no Dhandho-style mispricing or temporary distress; the shares trade at about 27 times earnings after a 37% one-year rise. Pabrai's 'heads I win, tails I don't lose much' setup at a deep discount is not present.
summaries.wood: Coca-Cola is not involved in any of ARK's innovation platforms (AI, robotics, energy storage, blockchain or genomic sequencing), and its market grows slowly. It does not fit Cathie Wood's approach.
summaries.ackman: Coca-Cola matches many Pershing Square criteria: simple, predictable, free-cash-flow generative, with high barriers to entry and limited exposure to outside forces. Ackman would likely find the price unattractive at about 27 times earnings, as he looks for a meaningful discount to intrinsic value.
summaries.sleep: Coca-Cola has the durable brand Nick Sleep valued, but it is not a 'scale economies shared' business: it uses its scale to raise prices and margins rather than pass savings to customers. Its position in 10-20 years looks secure but not clearly stronger than today.
summaries.valentine: Coca-Cola is a 140-year-old company in a mature market, not a fast-growing new market driven by technology. It sits outside Don Valentine's venture approach.
summaries.nash: Coca-Cola fails several of Nash's hard filters: revenue grew only 2% in 2025, total debt ($45,492M) far exceeds cash ($13,872M), and it is a mature business without a secular-trend tailwind. It does score well on margins, moat, pricing power, earnings beats and low short interest, reaching a borderline 75 on the scorecard, but the DCF at a 12% discount rate is far below the share price.

momentum.evidence: KO rose 37.38% over the 52 weeks to Oct 14, 2026 (about $91.60), well ahead of the SPY S&P 500 ETF's 17.28% one-year total return.

g4.evidence: Coca-Cola is run by long-tenured managers (CEO Henrique Braun, executive chairman James Quincey) and Warren Buffett's Berkshire Hathaway has owned it since 1988, holding 400 million shares.

g6.evidence: At about 27 times trailing and 26.5 times forward earnings (StockAnalysis, Oct 2026), some commentators call KO expensive for a slow-growing staple, though it is not widely labelled a bubble.

simple.evidence: It sells drink concentrates and brands to bottlers, a business any careful generalist can understand.

b2.evidence: Revenue rose every year from $33,014M in 2020 to $47,941M in 2025 and the dividend has been raised for 64 consecutive years.

integrity.evidence: Management gives clear guidance and non-GAAP reconciliations, paid $8,779M of dividends in 2025, and handed over from James Quincey to Henrique Braun in an orderly, pre-announced succession in March 2026.

b6.evidence: It focuses on beverages, but some acquisitions have disappointed, such as BodyArmor ($5.6B in 2021, later impaired) and Costa Coffee.

roic.evidence: Coca-Cola earns ROIC of about 20% and ROE of about 42% (StockAnalysis), although its debt of $45,492M flatters the return on equity.

fcf.evidence: Trailing free cash flow to July 3, 2026 was $14,297M, about equal to net income of $14,316M, but 2025 free cash flow was only $5,296M because of the roughly $6B fairlife contingent payment.

b10.evidence: Coca-Cola pays out most of its earnings, and the modest retained earnings have supported a rise in net income from $7,747M in 2020 to $13,107M in 2025 and a market value of about $394B.

safety.evidence: At about $91.60 the shares trade at about 27 times trailing EPS and 10.7 times book value, leaving no clear margin of safety.

fairprice.evidence: A forward P/E of about 26.5 is high for 9-10% guided comparable EPS growth (PEG about 3.6), though a premium is usual for its quality and stability.

mu5.evidence: With brands sold in more than 200 countries, a franchised bottling system and diverse categories, the main failure paths are slow erosion from health trends or tax litigation, not collapse.

reinvest.evidence: Capital spending was only $2,112M in 2025 versus dividends of $8,779M, because the asset-light model offers few large high-return reinvestment opportunities.

ly2.evidence: Coca-Cola is a classic stalwart: steady mid-single-digit organic revenue growth, high margins and rising dividends.

ly3.evidence: Its trailing P/E of about 27 is far above its earnings growth rate (comparable EPS growth guided at 9-10% for 2026).

runway.evidence: Emerging markets such as India, Africa and Southeast Asia still have low per-capita consumption, but global unit case volume was flat in 2025.

ly7.evidence: There is no notable open-market insider buying, and the diluted share count was little changed (4,323M in 2020 vs 4,313M in 2025, down 0.09% year on year).

ly8.evidence: Coca-Cola is one of the most widely owned and covered stocks in the world, with 67% institutional ownership.

fi2.evidence: It keeps launching and buying new products (Coke Zero Sugar reformulations, fairlife, BodyArmor, alcoholic ready-to-drink), though many are line extensions.

fi3.evidence: Product innovation such as fairlife and Coke Zero Sugar has driven growth, but Coca-Cola does not report large R&D spending and its innovation is mostly marketing-led.

fi4.evidence: Coca-Cola is one of the world's best marketers and, with its bottlers, gained value share in total nonalcoholic ready-to-drink beverages in 2025 and Q2 2026.

longterm.evidence: Management has invested for the long term through refranchising and brand building, but it is a mature company focused on steady EPS growth rather than bold innovation.

gr1.evidence: Coca-Cola has $47,941M of 2025 revenue and a market value of about $394B.

ni10.evidence: Coca-Cola has been profitable every year for the last ten years, with net income attributable of $13,107M in 2025.

gr4.evidence: Coca-Cola has paid a dividend every year since 1920 and has raised it for 64 consecutive years.

eps10.evidence: Diluted EPS rose from $1.67 in 2015 to $3.04 in 2025, an increase of about 82%.

gr6.evidence: At about $91.60 the price is about 34 times the 2023-2025 average diluted EPS of $2.66.

gr7.evidence: A P/E of about 27.1 times a P/B of about 10.7 gives roughly 290, far above Graham's 22.5 limit.

th1.evidence: Coca-Cola's advantage is its brand and distribution, not proprietary technology ten times better than rivals.

timing.evidence: Rising consumption in emerging markets helps, but health trends, sugar taxes and GLP-1 drugs work against sugary drinks in developed markets.

th3.evidence: Coca-Cola started by dominating the small soda-fountain cola market in Atlanta in the 1880s and expanded into a global leader in soft drinks.

team.evidence: Its management is experienced and well-regarded (Quincey grew comparable EPS steadily from 2017 to 2026), but it is a professional team rather than an exceptional founder-led one.

th5.evidence: Its global system of independent bottlers such as Coca-Cola FEMSA, Coca-Cola HBC and Coca-Cola Europacific Partners gives it distribution few rivals can match.

durable.evidence: Coca-Cola has led soft drinks for over a century, and its brands and bottler network make its position very likely to hold for another 10-20 years.

th7.evidence: Its opportunity is well understood by everyone; there is no hidden secret.

trend.evidence: Coca-Cola is not a leading beneficiary of a major platform shift such as AI or cloud computing.

dr1.evidence: Comparable EPS grew 11% in Q2 2026 and full-year guidance was raised to 9-10% growth, but Zacks reported estimates trending down after the release.

dr2.evidence: Completing the sale of African bottling operations and refranchising should lift margins, but this is already widely expected.

dr4.evidence: As a defensive staple it holds up in slowdowns and benefits from a weaker dollar, but high interest rates make its dividend yield less attractive relative to bonds.

dr6.evidence: The pending CCBA (African bottlers) sale, the 2026 FIFA World Cup sponsorship boost and a possible favourable resolution of the IRS tax case are identifiable catalysts.

dr7.evidence: Buffett has held it as a large concentrated position for decades, but its slow growth makes it more of a defensive core holding than a high-conviction bet.

gm.evidence: Gross margin was 61.6% in 2025 ($29,544M on $47,941M of revenue), up from 59.3% in 2020.

fcfyield.evidence: The free-cash-flow yield is about 3.6% (StockAnalysis), reasonable for a stable staple but not cheap.

gb2.evidence: EV/EBIT is about 26.5, an operating earnings yield of only about 3.8% on an enterprise value of about $422B.

pa2.evidence: There is no significant temporary setback: Q2 2026 brought 5% volume growth and raised guidance.

pa4.evidence: With dominant brands, low beta (0.32) and 64 years of dividend growth, the chance of permanent loss of the business is small, though overpaying is a risk.

wo1.evidence: Coca-Cola is not a leader in AI, robotics, energy storage, blockchain or multiomic sequencing.

wo2.evidence: Beverage costs do not fall quickly with volume; Coca-Cola has raised prices, with price/mix adding 4% in 2025.

wo3.evidence: It does not combine several innovation platforms.

wo4.evidence: The beverage market grows in the low-to-mid single digits, so it cannot become many times larger in five years.

ac3.evidence: Its asset-light concentrate model limits commodity exposure, but sugar, aluminium and currency swings still affect results since most revenue comes from outside the US.

ns1.evidence: Coca-Cola uses its scale to raise prices and margins (gross margin up from 59.3% to 61.6% over 2020-2025) rather than pass savings to customers.

ns4.evidence: Its position is likely to remain strong, but health trends and energy-drink challengers mean it is not clearly stronger in 10-20 years.

va2.evidence: Soft drinks satisfy thirst and enjoyment, not a large, painful problem.

tn1.evidence: Coca-Cola is a century-old beverage company, not one built for a secular trend like AI, energy or robotics.

tn2.evidence: The market sees Coca-Cola as a mature beverage brand owner, which is exactly what it is.

tn3.evidence: It is a large-cap US company and not a small cap, Chinese company, commodity producer, airline, seasonal business or startup.

tn4.evidence: Revenue has grown every year since 2020 and it is highly profitable ($13,107M net income in 2025), passing two of three; it fails the cash test, with $45,492M of debt against $13,872M of cash.

tn5.evidence: Total debt has exceeded cash every quarter (end-2025: $45,492M debt vs $13,872M cash), although free cash flow was positive year to date in 2026 ($6.9B in the first half).

tn6.evidence: Revenue grew 1.9% in 2025 and organic revenue growth is guided at about 5% for 2026.

tn7.evidence: Revenue growth of 1.9% plus a 2025 free-cash-flow margin of 11.0% gives about 13, and even the trailing FCF margin of about 28.5% plus about 6-7% growth falls short of 40.

tn8.evidence: In 2025 revenue rose 1.9% while total costs and operating expenses fell from $37,069M to $34,179M, lifting operating income 38% to $13,762M.

tn9.evidence: It fails two instant kills: debt ($45,492M) exceeds cash ($13,872M), and revenue growth (1.9% in 2025) is below 10%; its operating margin of 28.7% and 1.37% short interest pass.

tn10.evidence: Coca-Cola is fighting an IRS transfer-pricing case that the Tax Court decided largely against it, with potential tax liability in the billions, and faces sugar taxes and plastic packaging rules.

tn11.evidence: Coca-Cola provides branded drink concentrates and marketing that help bottlers and retailers sell refreshing drinks to consumers, charging bottlers for concentrate; consumers choose it for taste, brand and availability.

tn13.evidence: Borderline total of 75: cash vs debt 0, revenue growth 0, operating margin 10, short interest (1.37%) 10, institutional ownership (67%) 10, revenue growing faster than expenses 10, 5-year return vs S&P 500 (roughly in line) 0, moat 10, CEO 5, pricing power 10, secular trend 0, culture and mission 5, talent 5.

tn15.evidence: Interest coverage is about 8.3x (2025 operating income $13,762M ÷ interest $1,654M), current ratio 1.46 and liabilities 2.1x equity pass, but assets excluding goodwill ($89,325M) are only 1.27x liabilities ($70,541M).

tn18.evidence: Henrique Braun has a solid operating record but became CEO only in March 2026, is not a founder and has no reported open-market share purchases.

tn20.evidence: Coca-Cola regularly beats estimates; in Q2 2026 comparable EPS of $0.97 beat the $0.92 consensus and revenue of $13.38B beat the $13.06B estimate.

tn21.evidence: There is no clown CEO, co-CEO, fraud suspicion or auditor change, but the IRS tax dispute and BodyArmor and fairlife-related charges cut reported operating margin in 2024.

tn22.evidence: Coca-Cola has $47,941M of revenue, strong profits and a stable share count, the opposite of a hype stock.

tn24.evidence: At about 27 times earnings and a 3.6% FCF yield the price implies sustained high-single-digit cash-flow growth, above the roughly 2-5% revenue growth the company is delivering.

tn25.evidence: Using a 3-year average revenue growth of about 3.7% and FCF margin of about 14.1% (2023-2025), five years of FCF and 4% terminal growth at 12%, plus cash minus about $31.6B of net debt, gives a value per share well below $91.60.

tn26.evidence: A forward P/E of about 26.5 is above PepsiCo's and a PEG of about 3.6 is far above 1.
